title: MB9-14999
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on October 30, 2018, rejecting his claim filed pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti. He appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on October 30, 2018, rejecting his claim filed pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

The RPD found that the appellant was not credible as to the basis of his claim, due to important omissions and contradictions in the appellant's evidence. The appellant contests the RPD's credibility conclusions and submits that the RPD erred in the analysis of his prospective fear. They ask the Refugee Appeals Division (RAD) to grant the appeal or to return the file to the RPD for a new examination.

In his Basis of Claim form the appellant alleges that on XXXX XXXX, 2001, criminal "XXXX" from the XXXX XXXX came to his house in order to kill him. He was able to escape to his uncle's house, where he XXXX XXXX because of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX His uncle took care of him and took him to XXXX XXXX where he stayed with his uncle's friend until XXXX XXXX, 2001, when he left the country by boat to go to the XXXX. The appellant arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2001, where he made a claim for political asylum. His claim was rejected because the claimant had not provided enough details.
In 2008, the appellant got married and had three children. His wife sponsored him but the application was denied. He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and claimed asylum on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

On the day of the hearing, the appellant amended his BOC to add that he had been an active member of the OPL from XXXX 2000 to XXXX 2001. During the November 2000 elections, the militias of the Lavalas party took the streets to oppose the elections results favoring OPL. Following that, the appellant underwent what has been summarized above.

Based on my independent analysis of all the evidence on the file, including the recording of the hearing, I share some of the RPD's concerns with respect to the appellant's credibility and find that the appellant has not established a prospective risk in Haiti based on his political activities.
The appeal is rejected.

The RAD is required to independently assess all the evidence and determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. In exceptional situations, where the RAD finds that the RPD had a meaningful advantage, it will defer to its findings and reasons will be provided in that situation.1 In this case, the applicable standard of review is that of correctness. ANALYSIS Credibility

Generally, a claimant's evidence given under oath is presumed to be truthful, unless there are valid reasons to doubt it. In this case, there are sufficient problems with the appellant's evidence to cast a serious doubt as to the credibility of certain essential elements of his claim, as explained below.

I find it problematic that the appellant failed to mention in his original BOC that he was a member of the OPL from XXXX 2000 to XXXX 2001, in light of the fact that this is the central element of his asylum claim and the reason why XXXX XXXX XXXX allegedly attacked him. I do not find the appellant's explanation for the late amendment, namely that he had been inadequately advised by his counsel, reasonable. Allegations against a counsel can be given no weight unless the appellant follows the procedure established by the IRB to this effect.2 I also agree with the RPD that his amendment to the effect that he was a member of the OPL is inconsistent with his asylum form IMM-5669 where the appellant only indicated that his political implication was as a "protester" against the Lavalas.

The appellant testified that OPL was eliminated in the first tour of the elections. This is, however, contradictory to his BOC amendment, where he says that Lavalas militia took the streets to protest the 2000 election results that were in favour of the OPL.

The appellant further indicated in his testimony that during the second tour of the 2000 elections, he became a member of the Independent Party and that he worked on immobilizing the population to vote against Lavalas. He was supporting the Independent Party's candidate, M. Arnold Dumas. None of this information appears in his original BOC, nor in his amendment. As such, I do not believe the appellant that he was indeed a member of the OPL, nor a member of the Independent Party.

Furthermore, the appellant indicated in his testimony that he fears the current XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and who would recognize him because they XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and he had XXXX XXXX XXXX of the appellant's sister. However, no mention is made of this in the appellant's written narrative. I agree with this RPD that it is not reasonable for the appellant to have omitted this information which relates directly to the risk he would face if he returned to Haiti, especially in light of the fact that his asylum claim in the United States had been rejected for lack of sufficient details. Furthermore, according to the documentary evidence, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not the current XXXX XXXX, but rather the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Based on the foregoing, I am of the view that the appellant adjusted his testimony in order to amplify the risk faced. I therefore do not believe that the appellant had a close relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that the latter poses a risk to the appellant if he returned to Haiti.

However, even if I were to accept these allegations as being true, I am of the view that the appellant has not established a prospective risk, if he returned to Haiti, as explained below. Prospective risk

It is worth mentioning that the analysis of the risk that a claimant faces in their country of origin is prospective in nature. That means that the tribunal must evaluate if, on the basis of the events lived by the appellant, his personal profile and the objective country documentation, the tribunal arrives at the conclusion that the appellant has established that he will be exposed to a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, to any of the risks enumerated in section 97 of the Act, namely a risk to his life, torture or cruel and inhumane treatments or punishments, should he return to his country.

A significant issue is this case is the degree to which the appellant faces a prospective risk in Haiti. The documentary evidence does not establish that the appellant's profile, his past or future political work with the OPL would put him at risk as defined in sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

Firstly, the events as related by the appellant took place almost 20 years ago. The appellant has not established that he is still being actively sought by the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Even if I accept that he was a member of the OPL from XXXX 2000 to XXXX 2001, or of the Independent Party, the appellant has not established that he has continued to be implicated in Haitian politics, nor has he expressed a desire to do so if he was to return to Haiti. In fact, the appellant testified that he believed that OPL doe not exist anymore, which is contrary to the documentary evidence.3

Although election violence and instances of intimidation occur, the documentary evidence does not support the conclusion that political activity with the OPL would put him at risk of persecution or other serious mistreatment. The documentary evidence does indicate that armed gangs called "XXXX" who supported Aristide's return to power in early 2000 were responsible for "acts of terror".4 However, the documentary evidence does not establish a serious possibility that the violence lived by the appellant then is likely to occur again because of his past activities with the OPL or with the Independent Party.

According to a report by the Office Français de protection des réfugiés et apatrides, dated 2017, the tendency towards political violence has diminished substantially in recent years. There is currently no systemic oppression of political opposition in Haiti, who are able to enjoy their civil and political rights freely.5 The National Human Rights Defense Network, an NGO that monitors human rights violations committed by the state in Haiti, is not aware of current persecution against OPL members in Haiti. Furthermore, as per a representative of the Platform of Haitian Human Rights Organizations "there are a number of general protection problems in Haiti, but there are no more problems for this party [OPL] than for others". The same source stated that the POHDH has no files concerning OPL members, but "[that] some OPL members have been victims of generalized violence".6

I am of the view that the appellant has not established that he has a political profile such that he would risk being a victim of political violence, other than the generalized evidence experienced by all Haitians. Even if I were to accept that he will be recognized by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX if he returns to Haiti, there is no evidence that the latter would harm the appellant for his alleged implication with the OPL or the Independent Party two decades ago.
The RPD was correct in concluding that the appellant does not have a well-founded fear or persecution.

Pursuant to subsection 111 (1) (a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD pursuant to which the appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Act.

The appeal is dismissed. (signed) Bianca Eleonora Suciu Me Bianca Eleonora Suciu March 16, 2020 Date BES/tm 1. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v.
